# Numerically Stable Softmax and Log-Softmax

Naive softmax overflows for logits above ~88 (fp32) or ~11 (fp16) — a regular occurrence in trained models. The stable implementation is mathematically equivalent but produces correct results for any logit magnitude.

## The Naive Softmax Failure Mode

For $x = [1000, 1001, 1002]$: $e^{1000} = \infty$ in fp32. Denominator $= \infty$. Result $= \text{NaN}$. Training collapses silently.

## The Stable Softmax: Subtract the Maximum

Softmax is **shift-invariant**: $\text{softmax}(x + c) = \text{softmax}(x)$ for any scalar $c$.

Choosing $c = -\max(x)$: the maximum term becomes $e^0 = 1$ (no overflow), all others $\leq 1$ (no overflow), denominator $\geq 1$ (no division by zero).

```python
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F, numpy as np

def naive_softmax(x): e = np.exp(x); return e / e.sum()
def stable_softmax(x):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=np.float64) - np.max(x)
    e = np.exp(x); return e / e.sum()

x = [1000., 1001., 1002.]
print('Naive: ', naive_softmax(x))    # [nan, nan, nan]
print('Stable:', stable_softmax(x))   # [0.090, 0.245, 0.665]

# PyTorch always uses stable implementation
print(F.softmax(torch.tensor(x), 0))  # [0.0900, 0.2447, 0.6652]

# Stable log-softmax: x_i - logsumexp(x)
def stable_log_softmax(x):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=np.float64)
    m = x.max(); log_z = m + np.log(np.exp(x-m).sum())
    return x - log_z

# F.cross_entropy: log_softmax + NLL in one stable operation
logits = torch.tensor([[1000., 1001., 1002.]])
target = torch.tensor([2])
print(F.cross_entropy(logits, target))   # 0.4076 (correct, no overflow)
```

## Log-Softmax and NLL Loss

$$\text{log\_softmax}(x_i) = x_i - \log\!\sum_j e^{x_j} = x_i - \text{logsumexp}(x)$$

Computing via two steps (softmax then log) risks $\log(0) = -\infty$ for small softmax values. The direct formula avoids this entirely.

$$\text{NLL} = -\text{log\_softmax}(x)[\text{target}] = \text{logsumexp}(x) - x_{\text{target}}$$

Always finite and stable.

## Temperature Scaling in Softmax

$\text{softmax}(x/T)$: $T>1$ softens (entropy increases), $T<1$ sharpens (concentration on top logit). $T<1$ increases logit magnitudes — always apply max-shift before computing $e^{x/T}$.

## Attention Softmax Considerations

Attention scores $QK^T/\sqrt{d_k}$ can be very large. In fp16, scores above 11.1 overflow. **Flash Attention** applies the max-shift trick tile-by-tile without materialising the full attention matrix, combining numerical stability with memory efficiency.

Causal masking: set future positions to $-10^9$ (fp32) or $-10^4$ (fp16) — avoid exact $-\infty$ which causes NaN in edge cases.

| Function | Input | Stable? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| F.softmax | logits | Yes | max-shift internally |
| F.log_softmax | logits | Yes | logsumexp formula |
| F.nll_loss | log-probs | Yes | subtraction only |
| F.cross_entropy | logits | Yes | combined, one op |
| F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits | logits | Yes | log-sum-exp trick |

> **WARNING: Applying Softmax Twice is a Common Bug**
> F.cross_entropy expects raw logits and applies log_softmax internally. Passing pre-computed softmax probabilities causes log_softmax(probs) which is numerically incorrect and produces wrong gradients. Always pass raw logits.

> **TIP: Stable Softmax for Custom Layers**
> In custom attention or mixture layers: (1) compute scores, (2) subtract max along the softmax dim, (3) exponentiate, (4) normalise. Never assume upstream normalisation keeps scores in a safe range.
